query: Earlier studies of conventional metallic multilayers provide a general framework for deformation, but its conclusions may not transfer directly to high-entropy-alloy systems because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order are associated with unusual deformation behavior. Preliminary evidence from FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers remains insufficient to establish what controls creep or when a given response dominates. Within the constraints of retaining a nanoscale multilayer coating and balancing strength with deformation tolerance, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading? State what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would expose it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, boundary conditions, relevant prior support, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading in nanoscale FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings is governed by interface-mediated dislocation climb, where severe lattice distortion and short-range order slow atom diffusion along interfaces, making interface density the dominant control on creep rate.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoscale multilayer coating composed of alternating FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy layers, each 10 nm thick, random solid solution exhibiting severe lattice distortion and measurable short-range order.
generation.intervention: Systematic variation of individual layer thickness to 5 nm, 10 nm, and 20 nm (constant overall coating thickness) while maintaining identical alloy compositions and deposition conditions.
generation.conditions: Constant uniaxial stress of 100 MPa, homologous temperature 0.5–0.6 Tm, creep durations up to 100 hours under inert atmosphere.
generation.structural_mediator: Interface density (number of FCC/BCC interfaces per unit thickness) coupled with diffusion pathways modified by lattice distortion and short-range order.
generation.mechanism: Under sustained load, dislocations glide into interfaces and must climb to accommodate further deformation. Climb is diffusion‐limited; severe lattice distortion and short-range order in the HEA layers reduce atomic mobility along interfaces, so higher interface density (thinner layers) slows climb and thus creep.
generation.predicted_outcome: Steady-state creep rate will decrease approximately inversely with interface spacing. Compared to the 10 nm baseline (creep rate ~1×10⁻⁶ s⁻¹), the 5 nm sample will creep ≈2× slower (~5×10⁻⁷ s⁻¹) and the 20 nm sample ≈2× faster (~2×10⁻⁶ s⁻¹).
generation.baseline: 10 nm layer thickness multilayer exhibits a steady-state creep rate of ~1×10⁻⁶ s⁻¹ under the test conditions.
generation.boundary: Valid for layer thicknesses 5–20 nm, temperatures 0.5–0.6 Tm, stresses below macroscopic yield (<150 MPa), and random‐solid‐solution HEA layers without phase transformations during creep.
generation.uncertainty: Exact scaling exponent relating interface spacing to creep rate and quantitative impact of varying degrees of short-range order on diffusion coefficients.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate HEA multilayers with 5 nm, 10 nm, and 20 nm layer thicknesses; perform identical creep tests at 100 MPa and 0.55 Tm for 100 hours; characterize layer thickness by TEM and SRO by X-ray diffuse scattering.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If steady-state creep rates do not decrease with increasing interface density (i.e., no inverse relationship or the 5 nm sample creeps as fast or faster than 20 nm), the hypothesis is falsified.
